strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: non-invasive, 3D-spatially-consistent adversarial objects that attack BEV-based multi-camera 3D detectors without touching the target vehicle, which is more physically deployable than invasive camouflage attacks.

The pipeline is reasonably complete: automatic mesh placement based on bounding-box geometry, a differentiable-rendering-based multi-view/perspective-consistent perturbation generator, an occlusion-aware masking module (via SAM2) for realism, and a BEV-spatial-feature-guided optimization loss combining classification suppression, localization disruption, and scene-level feature confusion.

Experiments span three representative BEV detectors (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer) with white-box ASR across multiple IoU thresholds, and include a fairly extensive set of ablations (mesh shape, attack distance, random placement generalization, transfer across own-trained models, and range-stratified AP metrics in the appendix), giving a broad empirical picture.

Qualitative comparisons against the closest prior work (Adv3D) show the proposed method maintains greater scene integrity (less collateral damage) while achieving comparable or stronger targeted suppression, supporting the claimed contribution over existing non-invasive baselines.
The paper explicitly reports failure modes (e.g., weaker effect on BEVDet4D, degraded performance under random placement) rather than hiding them, which aids scientific transparency.
weaknesses: No physical-world or photorealistic rendering validation; the entire evaluation is in a simulated/digital pipeline (mesh rendered and alpha-blended into nuScenes images), so claims of being a 'realistic', 'deployable', physically-realizable threat are not empirically substantiated beyond simulation.

The 'black-box'/transferability study (Appendix B) only evaluates transfer among the three detectors used to train the meshes (i.e., cross-architecture transfer within the same small pool), not against truly unseen, independently trained models or different datasets/domains, limiting the strength of generalization claims.

The method's own limitation section acknowledges that (1) simply inserting an unoptimized initial object already perturbs detection somewhat (confounding the measured effect size of the optimized attack), (2) the attack is notably weaker against BEVDet4D due to temporal consistency, and (3) performance degrades substantially under random/off-training placement — these are non-trivial robustness gaps that limit the paper's central claim of a spatially/temporally consistent universal adversarial object.

No stealthiness or visual-plausibility evaluation (e.g., human perceptual study, comparison to natural objects) despite the paper motivating the approach partly on practicality/deployability grounds; the visualized meshes (Fig. 4, 6) show highly conspicuous, non-natural textured patterns that could be easily flagged by a human observer or simple anomaly detectors.

Key hyperparameters (α, β in Eq. 7) are fixed to 1 without sensitivity analysis or justification, and the interplay/relative importance of the three loss terms (Lcls, Lloc, Lsim) is not ablated individually, making it hard to assess which component drives the reported gains.

Presentation issues: numerous rendering artifacts in the text (e.g., 'i.elet@tokeneonedot' appearing repeatedly instead of 'i.e.'), suggesting a LaTeX macro error that was not caught before submission, and some formulation details (e.g., how B_{τ} indices are chosen among multiple objects, or how many/which target vehicles are attacked per scene) are not fully specified.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and relatively underexplored threat model: non-contact/non-invasive 3D adversarial objects placed near (but not on) a target vehicle to attack multi-view BEV detectors, which is more realistic than requiring physical modification of the victim object.

The pipeline is reasonably complete and well-motivated: automatic mesh placement relative to target bounding boxes, differentiable multi-view rendering with a dedicated occlusion-processing module (using SAM2 to mask meshes occluded by real objects), and a BEV spatial feature-guided loss combining target suppression, localization disruption, and scene-level feature confusion.

Evaluation spans three representative BEV detectors (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer) with white-box ASR across multiple IoU thresholds, plus a range of ablations (mesh shape, attack distance, placement generalization, transfer across models, sensor-range mAP) that probe different aspects of robustness.

Qualitative visualizations (image-view and BEV-view) support the quantitative claims and provide some intuition for why the attack works (e.g., pedestrian-like adversarial texture learned for BEVFormer).

Comparison against the most related non-invasive 3D baseline (Adv3D) shows the proposed method causes less collateral damage to non-target categories while still suppressing the target class, which is a meaningful qualitative advantage even if not universally superior on every metric.
weaknesses: All experiments are white-box and single-scene per-object optimization (mesh trained and evaluated attacking one specific target/scene at a time); there is no evaluation of a single universal object generalizing across many different scenes/targets simultaneously, despite the abstract's claim of "universal adversarial objects"—this claim is not clearly substantiated by the reported experiments.

The paper explicitly acknowledges (Sec 4.5) poor performance against BEVDet4D and weak robustness to random target placement, which are significant limitations for a method whose central claim is spatial/temporal consistency; these are described but not analyzed in depth (e.g., no ablation isolating why temporal consistency defeats the attack).

No physical-world or even simulated photorealistic rendering evaluation (e.g., CARLA) is provided; the "realistic occlusion" claims rely entirely on synthetic compositing onto nuScenes images with SAM2 masking, so the practical/physical deployability of the attack is unverified.

The threshold/criteria for what counts as a successful attack (IoU-based ASR ignoring category correctness) could inflate success rates and is not deeply justified; additionally no comparison to simpler baselines (e.g., a generic universal patch or noise placed at the same location) to isolate how much the spatial-consistency/occlusion machinery specifically contributes versus simply adding a foreign object near the target.

Reproducibility is limited by incomplete details on optimization schedule specifics (e.g., epoch/iteration counts per scene, convergence, computational cost/runtime), and no code/data release is mentioned.

The appendix transferability results (Tables 7-8) show fairly modest cross-model degradation compared to white-box results, suggesting limited practical severity of the vulnerability in more realistic black-box settings, which somewhat undercuts the paper's framing of a broadly dangerous universal threat.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and under-explored threat model: non-invasive, scene-level adversarial attacks that don't require physically modifying target vehicles, which is more realistic for autonomous driving deployment than invasive patch/camouflage attacks.

Technically sound pipeline combining differentiable rendering (PyTorch3D), a two-stage (2D + BEV convex-hull) occlusion-consistency module, and a BEV feature-guided optimization loss (classification suppression, localization disruption, and scene-confusion cosine-similarity term) that is well-motivated and ablated (Table 7-8).

Extensive experimentation: white-box attacks against three detector families (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer), comparisons against two relevant baselines (Adv3D, UAP), ablations on mesh initialization shape, distance robustness, number of placed objects, LiDAR-supervised camera-only model (GeoBEV), a simple adversarially-trained robust BEVDet defense, and transfer/cross-model evaluation in the supplementary material.

Physical-world proof-of-concept validation with a printed mesh and a real 6-camera-like capture rig, showing qualitative real-world degradation (mis-localization, false positives) and quantifying the digital-to-physical gap (Table 11).

Interesting qualitative finding that adversarial textures learned for different detectors resemble semantically meaningful patterns (e.g., pedestrian-like or traffic-cone-like textures), suggesting exploitation of dataset/contextual biases rather than pure pixel-level noise, which is a useful diagnostic insight for the community.
Reasonably clear writing and pipeline diagram; comprehensive supplementary material covering implementation details, occlusion-check illustration, and additional loss/metric ablations.
weaknesses: The comparison with Adv3D (Table 2) appears somewhat unfair: the paper itself notes Adv3D's initial (non-adversarial) baseline is already heavily degraded due to random placement causing severe self-occlusion, making the reported "drop" not directly comparable in an apples-to-apples sense; a controlled re-implementation with matched placement would strengthen the claim of superiority.

The main text mostly reports white-box results against models trained without adversarial exposure; the transferability/black-box results are relegated to supplementary Tables 9-10 without much discussion of why cross-model degradation magnitude varies, and no true black-box (query-limited or physically different architecture family, e.g., transformer vs CNN LiDAR fusion) evaluation is included in the main paper.

The physical experiment is a single scene/object type (car) with fairly limited diversity (weather/lighting variation is only simulated digitally via the TV-loss augmentation, not tested extensively in real conditions), limiting evidence for real-world generalization across diverse environments, lighting, and object categories (e.g., pedestrians, cyclists).

The robustness-to-defense evaluation (Sec. 14) only tests a lightly adversarially-fine-tuned BEVDet (10% PGD-augmented data, 2 epochs) and reuses a mesh optimized on the non-robust model rather than re-optimizing against the robust model or testing more standard defenses (e.g., adversarial training with larger budgets, input transformation defenses, detection-based defenses), so claims of "bypassing simple defense measures" are only weakly supported.

The threat model assumes the attacker can place a large 3D object at a fixed, favorable, and known distance/orientation relative to the target vehicle in the scene, which, while more practical than modifying the vehicle itself, still requires precise physical placement and visibility; the paper does not fully quantify how brittle the attack is to more adversarial real-world conditions (e.g., partial mesh occlusion by unpredictable objects, extreme distances beyond 3m tested, or vehicle motion/orientation changes across frames).

Some quantitative details are inconsistent or hard to verify: e.g., ASR thresholds and object placement choices vary across tables and are described tersely, and Table 16 has some presentation/formatting issues (small font, some entries seem truncated or hard to read).

The core algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior camouflage/Adv3D-style work — the main new contributions are the occlusion-aware compositing module and the BEV cosine-similarity scene-confusion loss, both relatively simple engineering additions layered onto known differentiable-rendering adversarial pipelines.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated threat model: a non-invasive, 3D-consistent 'environment-manipulation' adversarial object that does not require physical access to the target vehicle, addressing a practical gap relative to invasive camouflage attacks and prior inconsistent NeRF-pasted attacks (Adv3D).

Technically sound pipeline combining differentiable mesh rendering (PyTorch3D), a Realistic Occlusion Processing Module (SAM2-based two-stage 2D/BEV occlusion check) to ensure physically plausible multi-view/multi-frame consistency, and a BEV feature-guided optimization objective (target suppression + localization disruption + scene-confusion via BEV feature cosine similarity).

Broad and fairly rigorous experimental validation: three victim BEV detectors (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer), comparisons against two relevant baselines (Adv3D, UAP) with an explicit and reasonably fair discussion of confounds in the Adv3D comparison, ablations on mesh shape initialization, placement distance, number of placed objects, loss component contributions, and color vs. geometry contributions.

Physical-world proof-of-concept: printed adversarial mesh tested with a real multi-camera capture rig, showing qualitative degradation (mis-localization, false positives, cross-view corruption) that transfers from digital training, which is uncommon and valuable evidence beyond simulation-only results.

Additional robustness analyses in supplementary material (transfer across models, attacks on a LiDAR-supervised camera-only model, and a PGD-adversarially-trained 'robust' BEVDet) substantiate the generality of the attack beyond the main setting.
Clear figures (occlusion illustration, BEV/image-view visualizations, physical setup diagram) aid reproducibility and understanding of the pipeline.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single dataset (nuScenes); no cross-dataset or cross-domain validation is provided to support generalization claims.

The comparison with Adv3D, while discussed, remains somewhat imbalanced since Adv3D's baseline setup (random two-car placement, severe self-occlusion) already produces a much lower initial mAP/NDS than the proposed method's setup; the reported gap in attack effectiveness is not a fully controlled apples-to-apples comparison despite the authors' caveats.

The defense evaluation is limited to a single, relatively weak adversarial-training setup (10% PGD-augmented data, only 2 fine-tuning epochs), which may not represent a genuinely 'robust' model; claims that the attack 'bypasses simple defense measures' are only lightly supported.

Practical deployability of the threat model is only partly addressed: the attack requires placing the object at a fairly fixed, close offset (e.g., 0.1 m) to each target vehicle to guarantee effectiveness in the primary evaluation; although placement-generalization and distance-robustness experiments partially mitigate this, real-world logistics of consistently achieving such placement relative to arbitrary, potentially moving target vehicles in traffic are not deeply analyzed.

No assessment of the visual stealthiness/plausibility of the optimized adversarial textures to human observers (e.g., a driver or pedestrian) — several visualized meshes show highly conspicuous, unnatural colorful patterns, which could undercut the 'non-invasive/insidious' framing if the goal includes being unnoticed in real scenes.

The physical experiment simplifies the attack to texture-only optimization with fixed geometry, and the paper itself notes a performance gap between digital and physical results (attributed to color-space/printing mismatch), indicating the fully general (geometry+texture) attack has not been validated physically.

Some notation/equation presentation (e.g., loss definitions in Sec. 3.4, subscript conventions) could be tightened for clarity, and metric definitions (e.g., precisely how scene-level ASR is computed when multiple nearby vehicles are affected) are not fully transparent.
